titel: Brokerage accounts and brokers in the US
kurz: Who legally owns the securities in a US brokerage account, what SIPC and FDIC actually protect, how brokers earn money without commissions, and how to recognise a suitable broker.

bloecke.md:
A brokerage account is a register. In the US, almost all shares and ETF units are held electronically at a central securities depository, the Depository Trust Company (DTC), and are registered in the name of its nominee, Cede & Co. Your broker appears in DTC's books, and you appear in your broker's books. This form of custody is called holding in **street name**: you are the beneficial owner, even though your name is not on the issuer's shareholder register. As an alternative, many issuers allow direct registration with their transfer agent (Direct Registration System, DRS), but for normal trading street name is the standard.

This looks like a formality, but it matters if things go wrong. Under the SEC's Customer Protection Rule (Rule 15c3-3), a broker-dealer must keep fully paid customer securities segregated from its own assets and must hold a reserve for the cash it owes customers. If a broker fails, the aim of the liquidation is to move customer accounts to another broker, not to sell them off.

Cash is different. Uninvested cash in a brokerage account sits in one of three places, depending on the account terms: as a credit balance at the broker itself (a claim against the broker), as a deposit at one or more banks through a **bank sweep program** (a claim against those banks), or as shares of a money market fund (a security). Which one applies is in the account agreement, not in the advertising.

bloecke.titel: Two legal positions from one brokerage account
bloecke.unter: The upper path ends in a claim against a bank or the broker, the lower one in beneficial ownership; investor protection in the US also rests on this difference.

knoten.notiz: claim, FDIC or SIPC up to limits

bloecke.md: Fully paid securities in a brokerage account belong to the customer, regardless of the account value. Cash, by contrast, is a claim against a bank or the broker, and the protection of that claim has fixed limits.

## SIPC and FDIC

Two different systems protect two different things.

The **Securities Investor Protection Corporation (SIPC)** steps in when a member broker-dealer fails and customer assets are missing. It protects up to $500,000 per customer and separate capacity (for example an individual account, a joint account and an IRA are separate capacities), of which at most $250,000 may be cash held at the broker. SIPC replaces missing securities and cash. It does not protect against falling prices, bad investment advice or worthless securities. Many large brokers have additional private insurance ("excess SIPC") on top, usually with an overall cap for all customers together.

The **Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation (FDIC)** protects bank deposits up to $250,000 per depositor, per insured bank, per ownership category. Cash swept into bank deposits is covered by the FDIC only when it actually sits at an insured bank and only when that bank fails. Many sweep programs spread cash across several program banks to raise the combined coverage. However, any money you hold directly at one of those banks counts toward the same $250,000 limit there.

Shares of a money market fund are securities. They are not FDIC-insured, and SIPC only covers them if the shares themselves go missing at a failed broker, not if the fund loses value.

bloecke.unter: The chart deliberately contains no bar for fully paid securities that are on hand, because they are the customer's property and are returned; SIPC only fills gaps when assets are missing.

bloecke.md:
The statement "My brokerage account is FDIC-insured" is wrong in most cases. Securities are never FDIC-insured, and SIPC does not cover market losses. Cash is FDIC-insured only if the sweep program places it as a deposit at an insured bank, and only up to the limit per bank, together with your other money at that bank.

In 2024, the bankruptcy of the fintech intermediary Synapse showed another gap. Customers of several apps had money held in pooled accounts at partner banks, but the intermediary's records of who owned what did not add up. Deposit insurance pays when an insured bank fails; it does not reconstruct missing records of a non-bank intermediary. Investors who park six-figure sums after a large sale should know exactly where that cash sits.

## Three types of provider

Full-service brokers, online brokers and app-based brokers differ less in how modern they are than in how they earn money. The full-service broker sells advice and financial planning and charges for it through an annual fee on assets (wrap or advisory accounts) or through commissions and sales charges on products. Online brokers offer infrastructure: a very wide product range, research and all common order types. In October 2019, the large online brokers eliminated commissions on online trades in US stocks and ETFs within a few days of each other, and $0 has been the market standard since then. App-based brokers rely on simplicity, fractional shares and mobile trading.

Zero commissions do not mean zero revenue. Brokers earn from the interest margin on uninvested cash, from margin loans, from payment for order flow, from lending customers' securities, from fees and revenue sharing on funds, from options trading and from subscriptions or advisory fees.

bloecke.md:
## Payment for order flow is legal in the US

[[Payment for order flow]] refers to the rebate that a market maker pays a broker for routing customer orders to it. The conflict of interest is obvious: the broker might route orders to whoever pays the most rather than to where the customer gets the best price. The customer sees nothing of this on the trade confirmation, because the payment is contained in the execution price.

The EU took the opposite route and banned these payments. In the US they remain legal, but they are regulated by disclosure and by the duty of best execution (FINRA Rule 5310). Under SEC Rule 606, brokers publish quarterly reports showing where they route customer orders and how much they receive for them. Most retail market orders for US stocks are executed by a few large wholesale market makers off the exchanges. These must fill orders at least at the best price quoted on the exchanges and often fill them slightly better (price improvement). The SEC proposed in December 2022 to require auctions for many retail orders, but these proposals were not adopted.

bloecke.titel: Interest margin as a source of revenue
bloecke.md: The money market rate is set by the Federal Reserve's target range for the federal funds rate. How much of it a broker passes on for uninvested cash is not stated in any fee schedule. The default bank sweep often pays far less than a money market fund at the same broker. The difference is income for the broker and acts like a fee for you. More important than the advertised rate is the question of who holds the money: a bank sweep is a deposit with FDIC insurance up to the limits; a money market fund holds short-term securities, without deposit insurance but with very small price risk.

The end of commissions removed a visible fee, but it did not make trading free. Revenue moved to places that are harder to see: interest on cash, execution prices and product fees. Customers who opened an account years ago should read the current fee schedule and the cash sweep terms instead of relying on what applied when they signed up.

## Costs of a brokerage account

A cost comparison that only looks at the commission says little, especially now that it is usually $0. The costs arise in at least seven places, and the largest items rarely appear in the published fee schedule.

bloecke.titel: Three fee models for automatic investing
bloecke.md: The illustrative calculation assumes $300 a month, a term of 25 years and a return of 6% a year. Three fee models are compared. In the first, recurring ETF purchases are free, as is common at large online brokers. In the second, a flat subscription of $3 a month is paid out of the contribution, so $297 is invested. In the third, an advisory fee of 1% a year is charged on the account value, so the portfolio grows at 5% instead of 6%.

bloecke.unter: Illustrative calculation with $300 a month at 6% p.a.; the flat fee always costs 1% of the final wealth here, while the fee on assets costs a growing share the longer the money is invested.

bloecke.titel: Fees on contributions and fees on assets
bloecke.md: A fee taken from each contribution costs exactly its percentage of the final wealth, however long you save. $3 on $300 is 1%, on $100 it is 3% and on $1,000 only 0.3%. A fee on assets, by contrast, is charged again every year on everything that has accumulated, including past returns. In the example, 1% a year costs about 14.1% of the final wealth after 25 years, and the share keeps growing with the term.

## Moving an account to another broker

Switching broker does not require selling. Transfers between US brokers run through ACATS, the Automated Customer Account Transfer Service. You start the transfer at the new broker. Under FINRA Rule 11870, the old broker must validate the request within one business day and then complete the transfer within three business days. Many brokers charge an outgoing transfer fee; some receiving brokers reimburse it. Fractional shares and the old broker's proprietary funds often cannot be transferred and are sold, which can trigger tax.

For the tax side, the decisive item is the **cost basis**. For covered securities (shares bought from 2011, most mutual funds and ETFs from 2012), the old broker must send the basis information to the new broker in a transfer statement within 15 days. For older, noncovered positions, the broker does not have to report the basis to the IRS, and you need your own records. Moving shares between your own accounts is not a sale. Moving them to another person, such as a partner or a child, is a gift: there is no sale either, the recipient generally takes over your cost basis, and gifts above the annual exclusion ($19,000 per recipient in 2026) require a gift tax return, although tax is rarely due.

bloecke.titel: Worked example of a missing cost basis
bloecke.md: A position is sold for $10,000, and the actual gain is $500. With a documented basis, the federal tax at a long-term rate of 15% is $75. If Form 1099-B shows no basis and you cannot prove what you paid, the IRS can treat the basis as zero. The taxable gain is then $10,000 and the tax $1,500, twenty times as much. Keep purchase confirmations and old statements, especially for positions bought before 2011 or transferred from another broker.

## Taxes and foreign brokers

A US broker does not withhold income tax on your gains, dividends or interest. Instead it sends you a consolidated Form 1099 (1099-B for sales, 1099-DIV for dividends, 1099-INT for interest) by mid-February and reports the same figures to the IRS. You report sales on Form 8949 and Schedule D of your tax return. The only withholding applies if you have not provided a valid taxpayer identification number on Form W-9: then the broker must apply backup withholding of 24%.

An account with a broker abroad rarely makes sense for US persons. Many foreign brokers do not accept US customers at all. Foreign accounts trigger reporting duties: the FBAR (FinCEN Form 114) if the combined foreign balances exceed $10,000 at any time in the year, and possibly Form 8938. Foreign funds, such as European UCITS ETFs, are usually treated as passive foreign investment companies (PFICs), which are taxed punitively and require additional forms. For US persons, US-domiciled funds are the normal choice.

bloecke.titel: No exemption order, but a 0% bracket
bloecke.md:
There is no annual tax-free allowance for investment income in the US that you assign to a bank. Instead, long-term capital gains and qualified dividends are taxed at 0% as long as your taxable income stays below a threshold; for 2026 it is $49,450 for single filers and $98,900 for married couples filing jointly. Above that, 15% applies, and 20% at high incomes, plus 3.8% net investment income tax above $200,000 (single) or $250,000 (joint) of modified adjusted gross income. States add their own income tax, with large differences.

Losses are netted across all capital assets, whether shares, ETFs or bonds. A net loss offsets up to $3,000 of ordinary income a year, and the rest is carried forward without time limit. The wash sale rule disallows a loss if you buy the same or a substantially identical security within 30 days before or after the sale, including purchases in your IRA.

schritte.text: Look up the broker and its representatives in FINRA BrokerCheck and check SIPC membership. Do not invest any money with a firm you cannot find there.

schritte.titel: Find out where the cash goes
schritte.text: Read the cash sweep terms: credit balance at the broker, bank sweep with a list of program banks, or a money market fund. Check the interest rate of the default option, not the best rate in the advertising.

schritte.titel: Read the fee schedule instead of the home page
schritte.text: Go through all seven cost items, including the outgoing transfer fee, fees for foreign shares and mutual fund transaction fees.

schritte.titel: Check order types and trading hours
schritte.text: Check whether limit orders, stop variants and extended-hours trading are available and how fractional shares are executed. A provider without limit orders is unsuitable for larger purchases.
Check whether the ETF or fund you want can be bought automatically, on which dates and whether in fractional amounts, and whether it can also be held in an IRA at the same broker.
Check the transfer-out fee and whether positions can be moved via ACATS with their cost basis. Proprietary funds and fractional shares that cannot be transferred tie you to the provider.

bloecke.md: Almost every broker advertises margin loans or securities-based lines of credit, because they earn an interest margin on the existing portfolio. Under the Federal Reserve's Regulation T, you may borrow up to 50% of the purchase price of eligible stocks, and FINRA requires equity of at least 25% of the market value afterwards; many brokers demand more. The problem is that several things happen at the same time. If the market falls, the portfolio value and the borrowing capacity fall together. The broker then issues a [[Margin call|margin call]], exactly when putting up more money is hardest, and it may sell positions without asking you first. In this way, a temporary fall in prices becomes a permanent loss that goes back to a decision made months earlier.

mitnehmen: Fully paid securities in a US brokerage account are held in street name and belong to the customer; the broker must keep them segregated from its own assets.
SIPC protects up to $500,000 per customer and capacity, including at most $250,000 in cash, if assets are missing after a broker failure; it never covers market losses.
Cash is FDIC-insured only if it sits as a deposit at an insured bank, up to $250,000 per depositor, bank and ownership category, together with your other money at that bank.
Payment for order flow is legal in the US and disclosed in Rule 606 reports; zero commissions shifted broker revenue to interest margins, execution prices and product fees.
When an account is transferred, the cost basis decides the tax burden; without records, the IRS can treat the basis as zero.

begriffe.text: Standard form of custody in the US. Securities are registered in the name of DTC's nominee Cede & Co. and recorded in the broker's books for the customer, who is the beneficial owner.

Securities Investor Protection Corporation. Replaces missing securities and cash when a member broker-dealer fails, up to $500,000 per customer and capacity, of which at most $250,000 in cash. It does not cover market losses.
Arrangement under which a broker automatically moves uninvested cash into deposits at program banks or into a money market fund. The interest rate and the protection depend on the chosen option.
Payment by a market maker to a broker for customer orders routed to it. Legal in the US, subject to best execution and to quarterly disclosure under SEC Rule 606; banned in the EU.
What you paid for a security, including fees; the taxable gain is the sale price minus the basis. Brokers report the basis to the IRS on Form 1099-B for covered securities only.
